newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Little support for Kinshasa demo, bustle returns.
newsitem.headline: Little support for Kinshasa demo, bustle returns.

text.p: A march against the presence of Rwandan Tutsi soldiers among President Laurent Kabila's forces drew only a few dozen people in Kinshasa on Monday, as business picked up in the capital that changed hands two weeks ago.

United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan hailed Kabila for ending despotic rule in the former Zaire, and urged him to protect refugees and secure the rule of law in the country renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Kabila was in Zimbabwe's capital Harare for a summit of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), his first overseas trip as head of state since his troops captured Kinshasa on May 17 after a seven-month war to oust president Mobutu Sese Seko.

A few dozen demonstrators from a little-known group, not linked to popular opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, walked down the main street of the capital calling for Rwandans among Kabila's troops to leave Congo and for democratic reform.
But while many bystanders expressed sympathy with the "Forces of the Future", they did not join in.

"We cannot demonstrate every day, we have to make money to eat," said newspaper vendor Papy Baleko, who said he took part in earlier marches that also called for a role for Tshisekedi in Kabila's government.

Traffic was barely disrupted by the small march and shopkeepers said it was the busiest day in the teeming city since the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (ADFL) took control.
"People have to know why they are demonstrating and it is not clear that that is the case," Information Minister Raphael Ghenda told Reuters.
"Apart from that we should make sure that these people who seem to be gripped by xenophobia are re-educated in such a way that their sentiments are more fitting to our proud country."

Demonstrations have been banned by the ADFL and last week troops fired over the heads of student supporters of Tshisekedi, who says he is constitutionally entitled to the post of prime minister, to break up their march.
Tshisekedi's Union for Democracy and Social Progress says that it is planning more action to prevent what it says could be a return to dictatorship, but the programme has not yet been published.
At the OAU summit in Harare, Annan said Kabila, who has promised elections in April 1999, had a historic opportunity to set his country on a new path.
"We welcome President Kabila's commitment to constitutional rule and to the holding of democratic elections," Annan said.
But Annan also called on Kabila to protect Rwandan Hutu refugees and told him it was not too late to handle the refugee problem in a humane manner.
The U.N. Security Council, alarmed by reports of massacres of refugees, on Thursday called for an immediate end to violence against the exiles in Congo.
The refugees are remnants of more than one million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape reprisals for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Investigators have so far been refused access to suspected mass graves by Kabila's Tutsi-dominated army.
"Whether it is an official of the United Nations or whoever that makes these allegations they should not be made lightly and without verification," said Ghenda, when asked about Annan's statement.
